blocks.text: A Simple Model of Mixing in Shallow Estuaries

runs.t: Ada Rowntree
, Tomas Elling
Coastal Laboratory, Port Amble.
School of Water Studies, Hollin Vale.

We describe a two-box model of salt and fresh water in a shallow estuary. The model needs only the river flow, the tidal range and one mixing constant, and it reproduces the salinity measured at six stations within a few units. We fit the constant from one season of readings and test it on the next.

A shallow estuary mixes river water with sea water twice a day. Its salinity at a place depends on the river flow, on the tide and on how fast the two waters stir. Many models describe this with care; ours keeps only what a harbour office can measure. We call the salinity of box

The rest of this note sets out the model, fits it and tests it.
Equation 1 says that each box relaxes toward the sea value at a rate set by the constant k. The constant is the only number we fit, and the next section shows how.

We read the salinity at six stations at high and low water for one season. For each station we took the mean of the two readings of a day and the river flow of the same day from the gauge above the town. The flux between two boxes is then written as a sum of the river term and the mixing term.

blocks.text: F = Q s + k A r2

runs.t: Here A is the cross-section of the channel at the boundary. We fitted k by least squares over all days of the first season and kept the second season apart for the test.

blocks.caption: Figure 1: Salinity along the channel at high water.
Table 1: Fitted constants for the two seasons.

runs.t: The fitted constant changed little between the seasons, as Table 1 shows. The model followed the measured salinity at five of the six stations; at the sixth, close to the weir, it ran high on every spring tide.
We think the weir holds back fresh water that the model lets through.
